planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; set crowns just at soil level and mulch with leaf litter to keep roots cool and evenly moist.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from drying wind and afternoon sun. Keep the soil evenly moist through summer, since the broad leaves wilt quickly in dry spells, and top-dress yearly with compost or leaf mold to mimic its native forest floor. This uncommon Japanese woodlander forms slowly spreading clumps of rounded, peltate, softly hairy leaves on wiry stems, topped in early summer by loose sprays of small pale yellow flowers. It pairs beautifully with hostas, ferns, and other choice shade perennials as a textural accent in a moist woodland or shade border.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a fast-draining, humus-rich mix over rock or in shallow soil in partial to full shade; it grows equally well tucked into rock crevices, mounted on wood, or used as a low groundcover at the base of trees.

directions: Plant in a fast-draining, humus-rich medium over rock, bark, or shallow soil in partial to full shade, and allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings once established. It tolerates far more drought than most ferns thanks to its thick, felted, undivided fronds, which are simple tongue-shaped blades rather than the finely cut leaves typical of ferns. The rusty brown felt covering the frond undersides is a distinctive identifying feature and gives it real winter interest as an evergreen groundcover on rock walls, tree bases, or shaded slopes.

planting.note: Pot divisions in a light, well-drained, humus-rich mix and keep in constant high humidity and full to partial shade; this compact fern is best suited to terrariums, greenhouse benches, or shaded frost-free gardens in zone 10 and warmer.

directions: Pot in a light, humus-rich, well-drained mix and keep the medium and surrounding air consistently moist, since this small fern struggles in dry household air outside of a terrarium or greenhouse. Provide bright, filtered shade rather than direct sun, which quickly scorches the thin foliage. Its simple, glossy, dark green heart-shaped fronds on wiry black stipes make it an eye-catching, low-growing accent for terrariums, bottle gardens, or humid shaded courtyards in the warmest frost-free climates.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade sheltered from wind; give it room to spread its broad arching crown as the trunk slowly builds height over years.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade, protected from drying wind that shreds the soft fronds. Water generously and regularly, since it does not tolerate drought the way tougher landscape ferns do. Over years it develops a shaggy, fiber-covered trunk topped by a graceful crown of finely textured, soft-green arching fronds, making it one of the more elegant tree ferns for a shaded tropical courtyard or large container specimen in cooler climates.

planting.note: Mount divisions on a tree fern slab, cork, or coarse bark, or plant in a very open epiphyte mix in partial to full shade; let the flat brown nest fronds hug the mounting surface where they collect leaf litter and moisture.

directions: Mount on bark or a fern slab, or plant in a coarse, fast-draining epiphyte mix, in partial to full shade with good air movement. It produces two distinct kinds of fronds: flat, papery, shield-shaped sterile fronds that press against the mounting surface and catch falling debris as a built-in compost source, and tall, deeply lobed fertile fronds shaped like oak leaves that arch outward. This dual-frond habit makes it one of the more architecturally striking epiphytic ferns for a shaded tropical wall, tree trunk, or hanging display.

planting.note: Tie or wire rhizome divisions onto submerged wood or rock rather than burying them in substrate; site in shaded, slow-moving water such as a bog garden margin, pond edge, or paludarium in a warm, frost-free spot.

directions: Attach the creeping rhizome to submerged wood, rock, or a mesh mount rather than planting it directly in soil, since burying the rhizome causes it to rot. Site in shallow, shaded, slow-moving fresh water in a warm, frost-free spot, or keep it as a partly submerged bog and aquarium plant elsewhere. Its deeply cut, glossy, leathery dark green fronds hold up well underwater or in constantly saturated soil, making it a durable choice for the shaded edge of a water feature, rain garden pool, or paludarium.

planting.note: Plant divisions in a coarse, well-drained epiphyte mix in a hanging basket, mounted on bark, or tucked into a shaded rock crevice with accumulated leaf litter; give bright indirect light and steady moisture during active growth.

directions: Grow in a coarse, well-drained epiphyte mix in a hanging basket, mounted on bark, or tucked into a shaded rock crevice, and let the surface dry slightly between waterings. Unlike most ferns, its fronds are broad, strap-shaped, and undivided rather than finely cut, giving it a bold, glossy texture that reads almost like a broadleaf houseplant. That leathery, tongue-like foliage makes it a useful textural contrast among lacier ferns in a shaded tropical garden or as a low-fuss houseplant.

planting.note: Pot divisions in a light, well-drained, humus-rich mix in partial to full shade with high ambient humidity; it is best grown in a terrarium, greenhouse, or shaded frost-free garden rather than open dry air.

directions: Pot in a light, humus-rich, well-drained mix and keep humidity elevated, since the thin fronds dry out quickly in open air. Provide partial to full shade year-round, as direct sun quickly bleaches and scorches the foliage. Its glossy, palmately lobed fronds fan out like slender fingers or spider legs on wiry dark stipes, giving it a distinctive silhouette that stands out in a shaded terrarium, greenhouse bench, or frost-free shade garden.

common_name: Duke Gardens Plum Yew (Compact Spreading Japanese Plum Yew)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; give it room to spread wide rather than tall, since this selection stays low and mounding rather than upright.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial to full shade, and water regularly the first year until established. This selection is a low, dense, wide-spreading form of Japanese plum yew, distinct from the upright species in habit, making it an excellent evergreen groundcover or foundation planting for deep shade where few other conifers perform. Like the species it tolerates heavy shade, root competition from mature trees, and heat and humidity far better than true yews, and it is not browsed by deer. Its dark, glossy, soft needles hold their color through winter, giving year-round structure to a shaded bed.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade, mimicking the leaf-litter-covered floor of a limestone hammock; never dig from the wild, since this species is protected in Florida.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in rich, humusy, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in deep to partial shade, and mulch with leaf litter to hold moisture as it would in its native hammock habitat. Only source plants from reputable native-plant nurseries, since this fern is a threatened Florida native and should never be collected from the wild. Over time it develops a short, upright trunk topped by a crown of broad, finely divided fronds, giving it a miniature tree-fern presence that is unusual among the ground ferns typically used in South Florida shade gardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants to allow the spreading rhizomes to knit into a groundcover over time; keep evenly moist during establishment.

directions: Plant divisions in rich, well-drained soil amended with compost or leaf mold in partial to full shade, and keep evenly moist while new growth establishes. Its broadly triangular, coarsely lobed fronds have a distinctive halberd-like shape that sets it apart from the finer-textured ferns typically planted in South Florida shade gardens. Spreading gradually by rhizomes, it makes a durable, low-maintenance groundcover beneath native hardwood hammock canopy or in shaded tropical landscape beds in the warmest zones.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted stem sections in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in deep shade with high humidity; it scrambles and climbs over neighboring plants and structures, so give it room or a support to sprawl on.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted stem sections in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in deep shade, and maintain high humidity, since the delicate foliage browns quickly in dry air. Its sprawling, climbing stems root as they spread, so it works well scrambling over logs, pot edges, or other groundcovers rather than staying in a tidy mound. What makes it unlike any other spikemoss in cultivation is its structural blue-green iridescence, a true optical effect from thin layers within the leaf surface rather than pigment, which glows almost metallic in low light. It is a favorite for shaded terrariums and humid tropical shade gardens where that shimmering color can be appreciated up close.
